item.content:encoded:
If SCP-527 had the mental capacity of a fish, it would probably be easy to classify as Safe because its behavior could be routinely predicted.

IMO, it would still be Euclid because of ongoing maintenance requirements (as are nearly all biological entities). Obviously this is a controversial position, with no real consensus.

I suppose there could be an object class that meant "maintenance required; behavior predictable" BUT I suspect that it would not be as sexy as the plethora of Keter-scale classes that are popular with the novel object class boosters.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: To give some more detail on what my colleagues are trying to communicate to you, generally sentient humanoid objects are classified as Euclid because they cannot be predicted. If SCP-527 had the mental capacity of a fish, it would probably be easy to classify as Safe because its behavior could be routinely predicted. Sentient entities like Mr. Fish are capable of formulating escape plans, tricking people, figuring out flaws in their containment procedure, so the heightened object class reflects the extra caution that should be taken around things which can think for themselves.

SCP-527 was discovered in Boston by Foundation agents in 2002, and was moved to Site-19 in 2004.

This little tidbit just keeps bothering me in the best possible way, because I just keep envisioning what that precisely means. They saw him in 2002, contained him, and 2 years decided—for whatever reason—to throw him into Site-19 instead of Site-██? Or did like two Agents in their day off just go walking around NYC, like sitting at a cafe, look out a window, and just see Mr. Fish walking about?

Because, and I know it’s inappropriate and lolFoundation-y, just keep envisioning that Mr. Fish was just living out a completely normal life in Boston, with nobody even blinking an eye at the fact he has a fish for a head while some Foundation agents in a inconspcious Black Van with a Satelittle Dish trail behind everywhere he goes, looking at a clipboard and going “My god, who inows what this bastard could do!? I know that sure as hell probably isn’t what happened, but I can’t help but think that.

Still, a great SCP. Short and simple.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Obviously this is dividing opinions, and I'm with the crowd that is finding it difficult to choose between:

  • my appreciation for the meta-based subversion of expectations and the effort that was put into realising it (quite seriously, as the interview in particular has clearly been carefully crafted for maximum humorous impact and even a little character building in SCP-527's responses); and
  • the fact that this article yields almost nothing but that subversion, and makes no sense whatsoever in-universe. "The head of SCP-527 functions the same as the head of any other non-anomalous human" has no regard whatsoever to goldfish anatomy, the Discovery section raises more questions than it answers, and Dr Baker is a terrible interviewer. I know that this is the point - each of those things assists the humour - but while I am fine with humorous mainlist articles, this one breaks my suspension of disbelief.

Sometimes I downvote because I genuinely think that an article is not good enough to remain on the site. This is not one of those occasions - I appreciate what this is trying to do, and I think it does it quite well, but it just doesn't work for me.

item.content:encoded:
Personally I don't take the locked box test that literally. A potted plant requires you to water it and give it some sun, but that doesn't make it Euclid.

As far as I'm concerned, any living thing with generally normal physical/mental attributes for its species and no anomalous features that are poorly-understood enough or dangerous enough to present a significant threat is Safe.

If it's, say, more intelligent than we can grasp, or able to bend spacetime, or even just able to connect to the Internet (see SCP-2360) then it merits an upgrade.
